Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99 BC – 55 BC) was a Roman poet and philosopher. His major work is De Rerum Natura, On the Nature of Things, which is considered by some to be the greatest masterpiece of Latin verse.

In Latin:

Nec prorsum vitam ducendo demimus hilum tempore de mortis nec delibare valemus.

This is the first time I've seen the original Latin phrase be longer than it's English translation. And I changed "jot" to "moment" because I felt it read better.
"By protracting life, we do not deduct one moment from the duration of death." -Lucretius

Marcus Aurelius makes a similar point in Meditations II, 14:

Even if you're going to live three thousand more years, or ten times that, remember you cannot lose another life than the one you're living now, or live another one than the one you're losing. The longest amounts to the same as the shortest. The present is the same for everyone; its loss is the same for everyone; and it should be clear that a brief instant is all that is lost. For you can't lose either the past or the future; how could you lose what you don't have?

I'm sure it's no coincidence as he was a Stoic and Lucretius was an Epicurean. Those two schools were bitter rivals for the most part, but they borrowed some ideas from each other.
